utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usual routine, every morning. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours. Good morning. My name is Cayley. I appear with my co-counsel Nicholas Koumjian on behalf of the Prosecution. Our case manager today is Ruth Karper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cayley and Co. And for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Ms. Tania Radosavljevic and Milka Maglov, my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. For General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Xavier de Roux, attorney at law. I'm assisted by Ms. Natasha Fauveau and Mr. Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. So before we start, you know that tomorrow you have this informal meeting between you, which will be chaired by the SLO, the senior legal officer, Mr. Von Hebel. I don't need to remind you what it is all about, because this was more or less agreed upon in the beginning. But we're talking -- we will be discussing organisational matters relating to the Banja Luka chapter of this case. This meeting has been set for tomorrow, as I already told you and as you already know, and it will be held downstairs just behind or in front of Courtroom I in room 177. I suppose you are familiar with this room, room 177. As soon as you come out of Courtroom I, this is a room which buffers -- is in the buffer zone between the courtroom and the Judge's chambers. So you shouldn't find it too difficult to locate. It's at the end of the corridor which leads to then the staircase which brings you up to this one. The meeting is at 2.15, at 2.15, in other words, half an hour after we finish hearing here, and it's expected to last for about two hours. Obviously it will last less if the whole procedure is speeded up. And I understand also that there has been some consultation going on in the past days or weeks, as a result of which it's agreed that basically this is not a formal meeting but an informal meeting, and it will be certainly no disrespect for the beautiful French language, but this will be held in English, and there are no arrangements for interpretation. Okay? So that is the position. I'll move to the next stage. Does any of the counsel wish to raise any matter before we proceed with the evidence of Mr. Krzic? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion or disagreement about our future sitting schedule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I had understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have the schedule here with me, but I was looking through it yesterday, through June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm only concerned about next week. I had understood, when we discussed this matter many, many days ago, that we would not be sitting on the 11th, 12th and 13th. This courtroom schedule indicates that we are sitting on the 13th, which is, I don't think, the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you had told me that you will do your best to fly back on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember that very vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and then after that, I believe, Your Honour, you said, "Well, we'll take the 13th in any event, to give you an opportunity to then spend some preparation time once you return," but I will do whatever you ask me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I keep my word. I come from an area of the world where our word is our bond. So I will have the Registrar check the transcript of when we actually -- I think it was either the second day or the last day of the Pre-Trial Conference when we discussed this. I remember that we -- when we had organised the schedule for February and March, right through the 4th of April. Perhaps you could -- I do -- I do have a suspicion that Mr. Ackerman may be right. I'm not 100 per cent sure that you are right. I remember -- the only thing that I remember for sure is that you had told us that you will do your best to come back on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I definitely said that, but I'm old, as you know, and so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We both are, Mr. Ackerman. So we remember a part and forget the rest. So I will definitely check, and I will come back to you on this at some later point in time during this morning's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I also understand that Friday of next week is a court maintenance day or something like that and we will not be sitting then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which I was not aware of at the time, but if you mean by that that you're going to suggest that we also don't sit on the 14th, you're mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I just want to know when we are going to be sitting so I can be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being, according to the schedule, we are resuming on the 13th. But you may be right. You may be right. I will have that checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to start on the 13th. You have to make a big sacrifice, leave beautiful Sarajevo or wherever you're going to be and come back on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all right, I will just leave early. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But I will check just the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where I had given the extra day was, I think, either beginning of March, the first day when we will be stopping, March the 22nd or the 21st, or the 4th of April. That's where I superadded a day, I think, if I remember well, because obviously this was not that much important of -- of that much importance to me. Yes, anything else, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want Your Honours to understand that I'm not asking for anything but information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I mean, I certainly have no reason to complain about anything or the way you have been behaving or conducting your case here. Yes, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a small point, whether we need to bring another witness for next week. I understand from my colleague, Mr. Koumjian, that he will take the rest of today to finish the examination-in-chief. The cross-examination may commence tomorrow. It seems we may only have a day next week. As you can understand, we are rather like air traffic controllers with aircraft backed up all the way to Sarajevo, and the difficulty is if we bring somebody in next week, it means that they are then either -- they are going to have to be here for a day, then fly back, and then be brought back the next week. Now, we can put Mr. Inayat on to deal with the Banja Luka documents but we may run short of witnesses unless you -- you can, of course, require me to bring a witness, and I will, but it can be problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine it would be problematic, and I have been seriously thinking about that because I realise basically next week we will only have two days. And basing myself on yesterday's evidence, I have my serious doubts as to how much we are going to manage, succeed, in finishing the testimony of this witness this week. I seriously have doubts. Perhaps at this point, before I think further and discuss it with my colleagues and come back to you, perhaps Mr. -- basing yourself on what you heard yesterday, which should -- you are senior lawyers with a lot of experience behind you. What you heard yesterday should more or less give you an idea of what kind of a cross-examination you require to make and how long you anticipate this cross-examination to last. You were very specific and very precise in the case of the previous witness, Dr. Donia. So more or less, if you are in a position to help us, that would put us in a better position to direct the Prosecution as to what is expected from them next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to share with the Chamber everything I know in that regard. Bear in mind that depending on an answer to a question, I may cut 15 minutes out of the process or add 15, so it's a little difficult, but my guess is that I will be all day tomorrow and one hour the next sitting in the cross-examination. That's my best guess, and I think it will probably come pretty close to that, but it could go much longer, depending on a lot of things, including how long the witness decides he has to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I personally anticipate that this kind of witness and his evidence will have, as a reaction, quite a lengthy cross-examination, to be frank with you. Mr. de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after what I heard yesterday and what we have heard today, that hearing will be necessary to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means you require one day?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: One day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, potentially, if Mr. Ackerman is going to be here on Wednesday, we then have a day, or slightly less than a day, if we are going to sit for two days next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will definitely sit for two days next week; that's for sure. The thing is this: While the witness is not here -- I mean, you noticed yesterday that I did interfere as little as possible because I gathered at the time that this witness, you know, I mean, has his own way of answering questions, and each time we stopped him, he co-operated. But within a minute, he was again unfolding a whole story. He is your witness, and I appreciate that in the course of his testimony you did try to bring him to order. He's not an easy witness, so I mean, I would suggest that you do it carefully. But I would appreciate rather than we doing it, I would rather you did. I will tell him when we start today that it is desirable that he answers the question and nothing but the question. On the other hand, I would suggest to you, Mr. Koumjian, in particular, because I understand you will be conducting the examination-in-chief, that at any time you are satisfied that he has given you or provided you with the answer that you were expecting or that he could give you, you would interrupt him yourself and tell him that he said enough on that particular subject -- topic and that you would like to move to the next question. I'm asking you to do this because the Chamber itself will feel much more comfortable if you do it than if it had to do it. Our reasons are -- the reasons are obvious. If we do it, we would be interrupting you. If you do it, you would certainly not be interrupting the Chamber and you would be helping the Chamber. And so that, I think, I'm speaking in a language that definitely you understand. Okay? So at this point, I think we could call in -- yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we just essentially wait to make a decision on whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think so. In any case, I mean, it's not a decision that needs to be taken at twenty past 9.00 today. It could wait another hour or two. More or less, you know, I mean, we'll see how it goes. Because yesterday's testimony could have been considerably shorter. But things happen. So could you bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krzic. Thank you for coming again this morning. You will be given the same paper that was handed to you yesterday, on which there is the solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you. And Mr. Koumjian from the Prosecution will be resuming his examination-in-chief in you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, good morning. We have a lot of material we hope to cover today. And in the interests of moving the trial along and finishing your testimony so you can get on with your own business, I'd encourage you to give short direct answers to the questions. If I need further details, I will request them of you, and we'll try to move your testimony along as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you start, actually, Mr. Krzic, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mean -- can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also would like to suggest to you that when you are asked a question, you answer that question, the whole question, and nothing but that question. It would help the Trial Chamber to address the issues that are involved in that question more precisely, because when you answer the question involving other topics and other events, et cetera, more than -- rather than helping the Trial Chamber, you would be confusing the Trial Chamber. So please try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask the Court for permission to suggest the following procedure: Mr. Krzic, sir, if you could when you are answering the questions if you could look at me, and when I feel that the answer is complete, I will give you a signal. That way I won't be interrupting the interpretation or interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, were you aware -- in Banja Luka in 1992, did you hear the sound of explosions at night?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the cause or the locations where these -- excuse me. Did you become aware subsequently after hearing the explosions of the locations of what kinds of places were bombed or where explosives had been set off?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In most of the cases, I would learn that the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And what kinds of places or establishments were bombed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It began with shops and business premises or local companies owned by non-Serbs. Targeted at the beginning were also various catering businesses, various cafes and restaurants, and then the houses. As for the houses and buildings within the city, in the town, I would receive the information the next day. However, in cases of villages, I would become aware of that only subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Within the city of Banja Luka, did you become aware of the nationality of the owners of those you mentioned catering businesses and homes that were bombed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would become aware of that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the nationality of those owners who were the victims of these bombings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of the urban area, usually those facilities belonged to Muslims and Croats. As for the suburban area and outskirts of the town, usually the owners would be members of the Croat community. However, later there were cases of Serb-owned shops to become targets of such attacks, which we interpreted as conflicts between different fractions, either politically speaking or between different criminal groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At some point in time, did the bombings stop and other types of abuses against owners of buildings begin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember exactly right now. I would have to consult my notes. But that would take up too much time. The information as to when these changes occurred, I believe that it was at the time when the first soldiers started coming back from the front line in Croatia. The representatives of the SDS at that time publicly announced that all the shops and business premises owned by non-Serbs would be transferred to those returnees, if I might call them that way, as a sign of appreciation for what they had done during the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So when the bombings stopped, did confiscation of businesses and apartments begin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the shelling, the bombings themselves, did not stop altogether. They were just less intensive. And the targets changed. This time it was local homes and houses. The purpose was to force the residents of those houses to leave. And those houses were not simply bombed with hand grenades, all various kinds of hand-held rocket launchers were used, such as the rifle-launched grenades, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just before I ask my next question, thank you for responding so well to the questions. I think the testimony will go much quicker in this manner. Sir, were you aware of an airplane that dropped something over Banja Luka during 1992, during the indictment period, that is after April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you -- what was it that was dropped from the planes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dropped leaflets which contained threats and requests that non-Serbs not -- that -- for non-Serbs to move out of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you obtained one of these leaflets and gave it to an international person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we received such leaflets or posters. Children would gather them because there were planes circling in a visible manner. They made several circles above Banja Luka. And as far as I can remember, we kept such a poster in our party, and I think, as far as I can remember, that it was a -- handed over to international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what did the posters or leaflets say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really could not repeat that now. I just know that it contained threats, and that it asked for people to move out of that area, which was supposed to be just for non-Serbs -- just for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So would it be correct that the threats -- well, who were the threats directed against?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The threats were directed against the non-Serbian population, but it never said "non-Serbians;" it always said "Croats and Bosniaks," that is to say Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the indictment period, which I will say now but not keep repeating, that is from April through the end of 1992, were you aware of efforts or incidents where non-Serbs were required to sign over their property within Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were such incidents too, but they were mostly incidents which involved them signing statements saying that they were voluntarily leaving Banja Luka. I know of several cases, they had to accept formal exchanges without checking -- without being able to verify whether the buildings involved in such exchanges existed on the other side. I could mention the names of some such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to mention the names, but just so the Trial Chamber understands, are you talking about exchanges of apartments or residences from Banja Luka to Croatia, for example?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if a formal agency was set up by the authorities in Banja Luka during the indictment period to facilitate these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The representatives of this agency even visited myself and my family to ask for an exchange, to carry out an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if this agency was set up by the authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, they represented themselves, they said it was the SDS party that was operating and in their -- later on, in 1993, that agency changed the name to the Bureau for Moving Away, and it was officially registered in the Serbian entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the nationality of the people that were asked to exchange their apartments and leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were of Serbian nationality, of Serbian nationality alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The people that were asked to leave Banja Luka were of Serbian nationality? Did I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were only Croats and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the indictment period, Mr. Krzic, were you aware of a vehicle known as the red Kombi, or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one case, I even made a note of the number plate, if that is of any importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear stories, in other words did you hear accounts, from other people you knew, non-Serbs, about the activities of these red Kombis? And if so, what did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were numerous stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to testimony about what he heard, unless we are provided with the source where he heard it from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a question Mr. Ackerman is welcome to ask in cross-examination. I understand that the source is something that the Trial Chamber will consider in deciding what weight to give to testimony and second-hand accounts. This clearly is a second-hand account. In many cases, I think the witness is probably -- I'm asking the witness about things that he heard over and over again from many people, so he may not be able to name sources, but he may be able to give that answer. Again, I think it goes to the weight. I will try to make it as clear as possible what the sources are in my follow-up questions, and I think that Defence counsel can also do that in their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think I have to overrule your objection. The way the question has been put - and I have read it again on my monitor - does not amount to the hearsay evidence that you are referring to, because the question is a very simple one, that is whether the witness himself did hear stories about this red Kombi car and related events. He is not being asked to relate what he was told. He is being asked for the moment to state whether he was given information about the activities surrounding this red Kombi. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you can proceed with the question and the witness is kindly asked to answer it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard about it. I know the names of people who had personal experience of this, such as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify one thing, you heard accounts from other people that you knew. Were these personal acquaintances and friends of yours who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever see this red Kombi at one of your acquaintances' residences or outside the residence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned a personal experience that you had. Did this experience corroborate the information that you received from your acquaintances about the activities of the red Kombi? In other words, was it consistent with what you had heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was completely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify something, your personal experience happened in 1993 and not during the indictment period, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not just talking about my personal experience. I'm talking about my personal experience and the experience of my immediate neighbours, so that it's also personal but it's also the experience of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In what were -- were these red vehicles feared by non-Serbs within Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We used to call these vans mobile torture chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic. Were you aware, Mr. Krzic, during the indictment period, of trains passing through Banja Luka carrying non-Serbs out of the region?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am. And I've had personal experience of this too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The personal experience that you're speaking of -- I see you referring to your notes, and that's fine, but perhaps when you find your notes, you could tell us. I don't know if your notes are numbered by pages, but you can tell us the first words on the page perhaps, if counsel wants to follow. But actually, first, Mr. Krzic, I think you probably can answer my question without the notes. Why don't you try without and then we'll see if you need to refer to them. I don't need a specific date.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agree. So when we were first informed there was a train at the train station in Banja Luka which contained displaced persons, expelled persons, who were being sent in an unknown direction, a group of responsible people who represented the Bosniaks gathered, and we went to the train -- we drove to the train station. We went there in two cars. I myself approached this train at a distance of about five to six metres. It was on the third platform. Mostly these were second-class compartments. They had wooden benches and windows. And there were some compartments for livestock. Their doors were closed. There were only small windows at the top of the compartments. Would you like me to carry on with these clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Approximately how many cars were in that train, how many separate railroad cars?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No less than 15, but I don't think it had more than 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after you got to the station and saw the train?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues stayed very near the platform, which was as long as the train station building itself. We came from the left side. We parked our car in front of the building, approached, and looked at the train. We noticed that there was a military unit by the train, wearing camouflage uniform. They were -- there were intervals of about 15 or ten metres between groups of these men. I decided, in spite of the objections of my friends, to approach the train, and at that point, I saw the faces in the windows of the train. They were desperate. You could see fear in their faces. There were women. I can't exactly remember whether I saw children there, but I heard children crying inside. In the last car, which was for livestock, I saw hands protruding from these cars, but I didn't see any faces. It was a small window at the top with bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The hands that you saw coming from the train that was normally for livestock, were those human hands?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you saw the people, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to ask them something, but a soldier approached me very rapidly and he said something, he threatened me, so I wasn't able to ask anything. I didn't find out where they were from, but an old man spoke to me from the window, he said, "If only you knew the terrible things they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have been doing to us." The soldier made me leave. They were shouting, "We are thirsty. We want water."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was shouting? Just to make it clear, who was asking for water?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people, the women from that car next to which I was standing, were asking for water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned. I acted automatically, reflexively. I returned to the station, to the platform, in spite of my friends' objections, who were standing by the side. I automatically headed towards the toilet. I knew it was there at the train station, and it was at the end of the platform. A cleaning lady appeared there. She was wearing a blue coat. I asked her for a pail of water and she filled the pail up with the intention of giving it to the people in the cars. She started moving towards the train, but a soldier hit her, hit her leg, she fell and the water was spilt. He turned to me and started threatening me. And I and the entire group, all my men, we simply left the train station very urgently, very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document I'd like now to show to the witness and distribute to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have a document now which I'd like to distribute. It's titled, "Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka," dated the 30th of September, 1992. And it's been pre-marked as P449A. That's the exhibit number for this Trial Chamber. And it's addressed to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mission team, United Nations, in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, do you recognise this document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it is English, I can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And does this document describe in it the experience that you just told us about regarding the train that you saw in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is contained here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the second page, labelled page 40 at the bottom, the first paragraph. Is that the -- describe the incident that you just testified about, or is this a separate incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event that I have just described to you is described in greater detail -- far greater detail in my book on page 114. I went into details there and describe what happened after that. And as far as the 23rd, 24th, and 25th is concerned, this concerns the cars that were at the train station and had obviously been prepared to receive new masses of expelled persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you check your book for the date of the train that you saw. And I want to see whether this is the same incident or a separate incident.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two different events are in question. On the 4th of June, that was when this transport occurred. This is when I came to the train station with my representatives, with my collaborators. And I have mentioned this on page 114 in my book. We mentioned this train -- I mentioned this train to Mufti Halilovic that very same even and Bishop Komarica. The document that you have showed me on page 40, the incident concerns other dates, other dates are involved. As it says here, the 23rd, the 24th, and the 25th. So this happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in addition to the train that you saw, did you hear about other trains of deportees passing through Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And that's an example that you have informed me of in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, then, the incident that you described involving the woman who tried to bring the pail of water to the train happened in June of 1992. And that was the only time that you personally saw the train's deportees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall where you learned the information that's contained in the document that I just showed you concerning the trains in September?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly from the train station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have informants at the train station that told you about -- informed you about such matters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just me but another two persons, because it was hard to get in contact with me directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So in other words, you -- there were informants at the train station that would inform either you or two of your associates about trains full of expelled people passing through that train station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you receive information about events that were taking place outside of the city of Banja Luka and, in fact, information about events taking place in other municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At one point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. de Roux, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to raise an objection, because I think that the witness should give testimony regarding the sources and not on hearsay, not on things that we don't know where he got the information from. We're talking about information for which we have no sources, no evident sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't think I need your response to that. No. Mr. de Roux, I don't think you are grasping the real import of the question. The question is more or less to establish whether the witness had a system of receiving information. The previous question was: Did you have informers at the train station? The next question is: Did you have informers here, there, as to what was happening? I mean, given the position that he occupied and the political involvement of the witness in the circumstances, he's obviously being asked this question to see -- to establish the then-reliability of the information that he himself can furnish. So at this present moment, the question is quite acceptable as it is. Of course, I mean, if he's going to repeat what others told him, then he may or may not be stopped, depending on what the information is, because that would amount to hearsay, although the rule, as I explained on a previous occasion, is not absolute. But this question is definitely -- he's not being asked a question which would amount to hearsay evidence. He's being asked whether he was receiving almost on a constant basis information from others as to what was happening in the region, in the area, with regard to specific activities. So you can go ahead with the question. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we have an interruption, I want to raise another matter. I raised it yesterday. I now must raise it again. The witness a few moments ago referred to his book again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 114. The translation that we've been given of portions of that book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Starts on page 1, and ends at page 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I can't tell what came from page 114 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I am in the same quandary. I suppose my colleagues have the same problem as you are. It being just one instance that he has referred to the book, I was not going to raise it immediately. But at some point in time I was going to ask the witness to have a look at this English translation or at least the Prosecutor to indicate on this document where this reference is to be found. I quite agree with you, Mr. Ackerman. We are exactly on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose you got the message, Mr. Koumjian? I mean, I don't have his book -- we don't have his book in front of us. We have an English translation of a part of it, with no cross-reference to the page structure of the original. So we do have a problem that Mr. Ackerman has rightly pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. I know that somewhere in the English translation -- I've marked that section --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the moment you can go ahead, and then you can tell us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At the break, if the witness could remain one moment, we can confirm the page and the translation he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you receive information, in particular, a document, from the SDA president of Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document that's labelled "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, County of Celinac, War Presidency," dated the 23rd of July, 1992. This document is marked in the English translation -- pre-marked Exhibit P450A, and the original B/C/S version is marked P450B. I'd ask this to be distributed. I have a second exhibit. Perhaps I'll distribute it at the same time. It's marked -- it's labelled "Personal Testimony." The date of the document appears to be the 7th of August, 1992. And it is marked in the English translation P451A and in the B/C/S version P451B. In addition to the title "Personal Testimony," it is entitled "Report of the Misdeeds of the Chetniks carried out in the local of Sanica Kljuc County."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you also receive information simply from individuals without -- who did not have a political title from municipalities outside of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm showing you first -- I think you have before you 450A. That's the Celinac document. Do you not have it? Perhaps I can just hand you my copy.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this as what was given to you by the president of the SDA in Celinac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was indicated to you when this was given to you, as far as what it was? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was a definitive confirmation of the status of the non-Serb population in Celinac. The status in this case can be described as a status of slave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The person that gave you that document, is he one of the individuals who is listed in article 2 of the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is under number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if you have in front of you - I'll hand you now - the second document, which is -- "Personal testimony regarding misdeeds of the Chetniks carried out in the Kljuc municipality" is the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- to this document. It does not -- the name of the person who authored it is not even contained in it. It includes a detailed description of some things that allegedly happened at a certain time and place. It's the rankest form of hearsay. I don't know how I could ever cross-examine anyone about it because we can't even know who the author is. And it's a perfect way, it seems to me, for someone to throw stuff into this case that can't -- in the largest stretch of the imagination, could not be classified as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian, what do you mean to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document clearly is hearsay, which is not prohibited by our Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not prohibited, but it also says "personal testimony." Testimony of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness can explain who it was that gave him that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what is this document? Perhaps before we ask the witness - if we ask the witness - you could enlighten the Chamber as to what is this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This document is a document written by someone from the municipality who went and wrote about experiences that were happening to non-Serbs in Kljuc, handed that testimony or this account of the experiences to Mr. Krzic to get this word to the outside world, and which he passed on to the outside world. It's one of many documents, and I'm only offering it as an example - I'm not going to put all of the documents in - of clearly second-hand information that Mr. Krzic received and passed on to the outside world. This explains part of his role and his efforts to get the word out. It also is relevant because -- and I don't know if I should be saying this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As long as this document is not being exhibited, or as long as you do not intend to exhibit this document to prove the contents thereof, it will be admitted. If, in -- if instead, you are going to use this document as an evidence of the events mentioned therein, then obviously it cannot be admitted, because to all intents and purposes, it is a document which is anonymous, purportedly drafted by a self-proclaimed group of refugee citizens from Sanica, and unless information is at least forthcoming which would make it possible for the Defence to verify these -- the reliability of these documents, and also cross-examine the persons who may have furnished the information to the witness, you will understand that this Chamber cannot admit it. So that is the position. If the only purpose of this document is to prove that Mr. Krzic, the witness, was receiving information from persons, identified or non-identified, as to events that were reported to him, then it's okay. But that is the only extent to which this Chamber will admit that document. Otherwise, it is, as I said, an anonymous declaration of events which cannot be proved by this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assure the Court that for all the specific incidents charged in this indictment, the Prosecution will present first-hand testimony from people who witnessed those events. But I would also just point out - and I perfectly accept Your Honour's ruling and understand it - that another aspect of this case that we are trying to prove in regards to Banja Luka and the other municipalities is the atmosphere of terror which was created sometimes not just by a direct experience but from second-hand information of what was going on around people that forced people to abandon their homes and leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are perfectly right, Mr. Koumjian. However, you have to understand, I think, that this document can only serve one purpose; in other words, that Mr. Krzic was being kept informed by several persons. He was sort of a key person to whom people were referring information. However, it remains -- it starts and remains a document which, to all intents and purposes, is an anonymous document, and therefore, it definitely cannot and will not constitute proof of its contents. That's being made clear by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, as a fact that he was handed this document that can be established in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, just briefly, if you could take a look at the original of that document in B/C/S, and tell me, if you recall, have you seen this document before, and if so, where did you see it or where did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received it personally in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd ask you to just take a look. I would just like to point out the second-to-last paragraph, regarding in this document, that begins, "That not everything is as black as it seems. Is seen among the numerous examples of self-sacrifice undertaken by the local Serb people who have rendered assistance, from hiding persons in their attics during raids to bringing bread to the jails and schools and many other acts which the Muslims of this region will never forget."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've just ruled that it cannot be admitted for the truth of its contents and now we are being supplied with its contents, apparently as a representation that they are true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. He hasn't come with the question as yet. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you receive information from non-Serbs outside the municipality, and within Banja Luka, that there were Serbs helping Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That closes your objection, Mr. Ackerman, because obviously, the situation has been clarified. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you speak to non-Serbs in Banja Luka who decided during 1992 to leave the city or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With non-Serbs? Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what reasons people gave for why they were leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first reason was that they felt their lives and their family lives threatened. The other, second reason, was the impossibility of living under conditions of different types of pressures, which I have already described. And the third reason was the impossibility of heating their homes, of obtaining food in the winter months. These were the main reasons why these people left. Also the forced call-ups, mobilisation. Well, I don't suppose we have to mention all the reasons. There is also the impossibility of obtaining medical care. People were jobless. They had property there, they had their usual life, and they expected all this to end one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were non-Serbs within Banja Luka municipality, to your knowledge, aware of camps in which opponents of the authorities were being imprisoned, or in which non-Serbs were being imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure the vast majority was aware of this. The public at large knew about this because the Serb authorities, in fact, came -- in fact, obtained the information that I sent out abroad, and broadcast this on their own televisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In late August of 1992, was there a very public information about a massacre that occurred on a convoy of non-Serbs passing over Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information about the massacre a day later from persons who were present at the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but my question is, to your knowledge, was this -- let me -- I wasn't specific enough. To your knowledge, was this publicised? Was it on the radio and in the media, information about this massacre?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, no. As far as I know, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you yourself have some information or some involvement in the situation that took place in a village in Kljuc municipality known as Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vecici, they are not in the Kljuc area. It is not a village in the Kljuc area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received, on a regular basis, information about events taking place in Vecici. I received information from the Serb authorities informally and formally, and myself, on one occasion, I was able to receive such information on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the situation as you knew it before you actually went to Vecici? What was the situation that was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole of Banja Luka witnessed daily flights of fighting planes that unloaded their explosives in that area where the people were defending themselves. Every day, daily, returnees from the front lines passed through Banja Luka, who were shooting in the air, throughout the city. I saw many vans and trucks of soldiers coming back from Vecici and Kotor Varos, shooting by way of celebration. I also received from Mr. Kupresanin, from the Serb authorities in his office, where other witnesses were also present. I also received the information in a concealed fashion from family and friends in the area of Vecici and Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, would it be correct to summarise the situation that there was resistance -- armed resistance by non-Serbs in and around that village to the Serbian authorities in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I forgot to mention that the information was also partially published in the Banja Luka press, in the propaganda sense, and such information also received from the police, the Banja Luka SUP, when I was arrested and when they showed me the special police -- the policemen of special forces who were killed during that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And sir, did you yourself attempt to get arms to the fighters -- the non-Serb fighters in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't have any arms for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you supported those non-Serb fighters in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I supported them in the moral sense because we saw what was going on in respect of the innocent population, this sort of genocide that was being carried out. And I understood that struggle as resistance of people, of men, women, and children, against this genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that arms were being sent from Banja Luka to the fighters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that some of the volunteers that went to Vecici took along arms with them. When I say "arms," I mean light arms. Some of them tried to obtain ammunition in Banja Luka and anti-tank weapons. They even approached tank brigades. But they didn't have anti-tank arms. I don't know to what extent they were able to procure such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it publicised that the authorities, the Serbian authorities, were demanding the surrender of these fighters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw such a document when an order -- when a visit was ordered in the area of Kotor Varos and Vecici. I was shown such a document on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kupresanin ask you to go with him to Vecici to contact the fighters there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately following the talk I had with the American representative, Mr. Galbraith, the very same day, I was sent a message by Mr. Kupresanin to come to his office urgently in the municipal assembly. When I came to the office -- I did not accept to do this immediately, but I was asked to come to Vecici and to ask the fighters to surrender. There were four witnesses present. I can quote their names, including Mr. Beat Schwitzer of the International Red Cross. Mr. Kupresanin did not come with me to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you went to Vecici, were you asked by some of the Serbian authorities to deliver a message to the fighters, and if so, what was the message or demands of the authorities to the fighters in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the presence of the representatives of the HDZ, a priest, and two of us representing the Bosniak people, a group representing the Serb authorities - I think I mentioned all in names in my book - headed by Colonel Peulic, they required of us to require -- to demand their unconditional surrender. A document had been offered where, as far as I can remember, some of the conditions for the surrender were listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you know, sir, do you know Colonel Peulic, what corps he was part of and who his superior was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was commander of the Serb army in the area of Kotor Varos and obviously his superior commander was, as far as I can remember, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When the authorities, Serbian authorities, and army demanded the surrender of the fighters, did they indicate what they would do with the fighters if they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- it was not explicitly explained in front of me what would happen to the fighters. It was said - and I mostly heard this from the HDZ representatives - that the population would be gathered together and collected and then transported to Travnik, I think. But I was not explicitly informed of what would happen to the fighters on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So when you used the word "population," you mean that the -- you're including non-fighters, civilians, would be taken from the area where they lived and taken to Travnik, which was in the territory controlled by the Bosniak government -- the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a document which we have pre-marked P452A in the English version and P452B in the B/C/S version. It is entitled "Party of Democratic Action Banja Luka," dated 18 October, 1992. And it's addressed to the Ambassador Muhamed Sacirbey at the Bosnian and Herzegovinian missions of the United Nations in New York. The subject line is "Ethnic cleansing in the territory of Kotor Varos."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm acquainted with that document. I signed it myself. I wrote it and signed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does this document report on your involvement in these negotiations in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does contain that. But it is a summary of what I believe to be important, to mention my personal report contains more details that perhaps could be relevant for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you were told to demand by the authorities -- Serbian authorities to demand the surrender of the fighters in the population. Did you in fact go and speak to the fighters in Kotor Varos -- in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was required to do so. And here I had no choice. So I decided to accept to go to Vecici but not alone. There were two other people with me: Mr. Dzumhur and the priest, Adolf. And in Vecici, we had talks -- well, we didn't know who these people were then -- that is, with three people representatives of the Vecici population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, whenever it's convenient for you, please bring this initial part of your -- of today's examination to an end so that we can break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you spoke to the fighters in Vecici, did they -- did you pass information from them back to the authorities regarding their response to the demands for surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. These answers are written in the same document issued by the Serb soldiers from Kotor Varos. On the second page, this was written in print -- the reply was written in print.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is that reply given in the document that has been marked, that you sent to the ambassador at the United Nations, that being that the fighters responded that the -- that they demanded an "all-for-all exchange of dead soldiers and POWs with the Serbian side, that the ICRC" -- that's the International Committee for the Red Cross -- "must come to Vecici in order to guarantee safety, that humanitarian aid be brought to Vecici, and that foreign reporters be allowed to Vecici."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you give that response to Colonel Peulic, and if so, what was his response?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I transmitted this reply to Colonel Peulic, in the presence of the other people I mentioned. When he read this, he shouted out, "We will destroy them," and he banged his fist on the table and everything shook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the words he used, to the best of your recollection? When he said, "We will destroy them," is that what you recall? Do you recall any exact words?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "We'll destroy them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The next day, did Mr. Kupresanin call you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say this with accuracy, whether it was that day or the day afterwards. I think it was the next day. I was -- Mr. Kupresanin called me. He was very polite at the beginning and inquired about Kotor Varos. And then -- then his words were very sharp. He even swore at me. He said that I had betrayed him, tricked him, and that I should go back to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vecici straight away and to see that these people surrender. If I refused to do so, then in the very next morning, I would be taken -- he would take me to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of what the Manjaca camp was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in fact -- it conjured in my mind a picture of liquidation. Me, with my reputation, I would never emerge from there alive. And not only an ordinary death, but a death accompanied by torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll break for 25 minutes. We'll resume the hearing at five to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. I recognise Mr. Ackerman on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the purposes of the record, and perhaps for the assistance of the Chamber, page 114 of Mr. Krzic's book is page 30 and 31 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman, as usual. As we go along, you are proving to be almost indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just hope Mr. Brdjanin feels the same way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I am sure that Mr. Brdjanin is completely satisfied with you as his attorney, as I would be. Thank you. Could you bring the witness in, please? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, you can resume the examination of your witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin -- excuse me, Mr. Krzic, you mentioned earlier that part of your role as president of the SDA was meeting with journalists and with representatives of international organisations and foreign embassies. What was your purpose in speaking to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the purpose was to introduce the work and the objectives of the work of the party in this area, as a political organisation, in a period of democratic changes. My wish was to convince them that, as far as the SDA is concerned, these changes are in accordance with generally accepted democratic principles. Second, in view of the overall exacerbation of the situation, it was my wish to acquaint them with the current events and some consequences which had more general repercussions. And thirdly, my contact with foreigners - and again, there were not only diplomats and journalists but occasionally, there would be some representatives, such as Mr. Galbraith and others - that is, the objective of my contact with them was to ask the representatives of foreign countries to try and save the population, the people, in general, from the very obvious attempts at their physical destruction. I simply had to use my position for that purpose because it was possible for me to act in that perspective, with that purpose in mind, whereas ordinary people, a man in the street, would have suffered severe consequences if exposed to such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to distribute two documents. They are labelled, premarked, P453A in the English, and 453B. This is a document that is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior, dated 6th of July, 1993, from the National Security Service Sector in Banja Luka, and it is addressed to the president of the regional board of the SDS, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. The second document, we have premarked P454A in the English translation and it is the 454B in the original B/C/S version. It is from the same security service. It is dated the 23rd of July, 1993. It is also addressed to Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, president of the SDS. And just for Defence counsel, those two exhibits are in order disclosures number 4.1237, and 4.1239. I'd ask that the B/C/S versions be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't yet found the documents, but they've been offered as documents dated 6 July 1993 and 23 July 1993, which is more than six months outside the parameters of this indictment, which ends in December of 1992. And so I cannot see that they would have any relevance to any issues in this case. Perhaps the Prosecutor can state what relevance they might have, but they appear to be completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection would have been exactly the same, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your reaction, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indictment concerns crimes in 1992. These two documents actually do not discuss crimes at all, but what they do show and go to prove is that the security service, and in particular Mr. Brdjanin, had an interest in the activities of Mr. Krzic and his contacts with foreign media and the fact -- foreigners and the fact that he was a political person getting the word out to the world about the crimes that had occurred since 1992 in the area. So I think it is very relevant to the knowledge of Mr. Brdjanin of the activities of the security service and the interests of the accused in hiding the crimes that had taken place. I would point out that any effort to hide a crime is going to be relevant, even if that took place long after the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the opinion that on face value, these two documents can be relevant to the point that has just been made by the Prosecutor, subject, of course, to the probative value that they would be given in due course. Thank you. So you can now proceed with filing or introducing these two documents 453A and 454A, and then we'll take it up from there. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, if you could briefly look at those documents in the B/C/S version. And is it true that you first saw these documents here in The Hague last week when I showed them to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The documents list several individuals that you had contact with, including Mr. Hamdija Todorovic and Veronique Pasquier, a Swiss journalist. Is it correct that you did have contact with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But let me just correct you. The name is Todorovac not Todorovic. And the other person is Veronique Pasquier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It also is indicated in document 454A that you had contact with some foreign journalists, including Mr. Roy Gutman. Is it correct that you did have contact and give interviews to Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, sir, in 1992, is it correct that you once had a meeting with Mr. Gutman in your home which was followed up by a visit from some other people to your home?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And after you spoke to Mr. Gutman, who came to see you at your home?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two police officers in plain clothes came to see me, within a very short period of time, one hour, an hour and a half, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did they question you about your meeting with Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And they made notes of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have some other documents to distribute. And it's going to be quite a group. First, Your Honour, we have pre-marked as Exhibit P455A in the English version and 455B in the B/C/S version a document that indicates it's from the Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka, dated the 2nd of August, 1992. The subject line is, "Report of a meeting of the SDA with the ICRC on 31 July 1992 in the offices of the ICRC." The next document we have pre-marked as P456A and 456B. And the original, it is indicated, is from the Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka, dated 18 November 1992, and it is addressed to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mission to the United Nations, New York, Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey, ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that these two documents have been disclosed to the Defence already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: All the documents that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- have been disclosed, along with the witness statements, so they are under disclosure 7.99. The next document that I have, we have marked P457A and 457B. It's indicated it's from the Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka. It's addressed to the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mission to the United Nations, New York, Muhamed Sacirbey personally, indicates on the topic line, "Report of a meeting with the mayor of the county council of Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just trying to shuffle my papers. I believe I was last at 456. I don't believe I've read for the record 457. I have a document marked, "Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka," premarked 457A and 457B. It is addressed to the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, mission to the United Nations, New York, Muhamed Sacirbey personally. The topic line is, "Meeting with the mayor of the county council of Banja Luka." Perhaps I did read that but I didn't find that in the LiveNote. We have as document 4.5 -- we have that already? Excuse me, marked P458A and 458B, a document that indicates it's to Mr. Vance and Lord Owen. On the original, there is not a date but there is a fax transmission date of 12 December, 1992, and it is on the letterhead of the Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Koumjian, I notice that document P457A, as well as its counterpart, P457B, do not show any date. They purport to be signed by a witness, and being supposedly a transcript or a copy of communication to His Excellency Muhamed Sacirbey at the embassy -- at the mission. I would have expected it to be dated. It's definitely subsequent to the 8th December, 1992, but that's as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. There is a date referred to in the first line, which is -- it indicates on the first line, "On 8 December" - of the report - "1992, at our urgent demand, we were received by Mayor Radic." Apparently it's a report regarding a meeting that took place on the 8th of December, 1992, with Mr. Radic, but there is not a date on the document, at least on the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the type of document which I would imagine was faxed. I mean, it's the kind of document that is not sent by mail. Usually it's faxed, as is the case with the other documents, or some of the other documents. I don't know. I'm just -- I just thought I needed to indicate that to you because, more or less, it's an important aspect that should be noted. Yes, please go ahead --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think I've learned my lesson to do one exhibit at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. In fact, I was going to suggest to you that you deal with these documents now one by one, while you are questioning your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because, I mean, it's not fair putting on his desk four documents, about 20 or 30 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- and I can mix up two pieces of paper, let alone this many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Going through these documents one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you, sir, document 455B, which is the 2nd of August, 1992, report on the SDA meeting with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I fully agree with this document. However, I must note that there is a certain difficulty in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but -- and I will allow you to explain, but first let me just ask: Do you know who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every document, including this one, which is actually a report of a meeting with international organisations, was authored by myself -- of course, in consultation with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through the contents of all these documents because the Court can read them and they speak for themselves. Is it correct, simply, that this is a report of a meeting by your -- members of your party with the International Committee of the Red Cross on 31st of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report that I have in front of me is exactly this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the next document, which is 456, it is dated the 18th of November, 1992, addressed to the UN mission, to the ambassador of Bosnia in New York, and is it correct that you are the author of this document? Your name appears on the signature -- on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you write the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this common for you to write to the embassy or to the UN mission in New York of Bosnia reporting on events that were taking place in the region of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do it upon anyone's suggestion or proposal; neither did we have any specific instruction from any higher level, the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example. It was done mostly spontaneously. We thought that that would be the best way to proceed because the mission was working at the United Nations, and we thought that that would be the best way to familiarise the international community with the current events.
