And in view of the remark made by His Honour regarding faxing, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. must add that a great number of documents were not faxed from Banja Luka but from another state, which it -- they -- which they reached in a concealed fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you could just explain that, or correct me if I'm wrong. Is it correct that for security reasons you asked some people to take these letters outside of the Bosnian Krajina region and fax them from other locations, such as Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the next document, 457. Again, can you confirm that you are the author of this document? And this is the -- entitled "Report of a Meeting with the Mayor of the County Council of Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Let me just note that in this document and in the previous document, we found something that is explained in greater detail than my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would ask you to note on this the paragraph -- there are three numbered paragraphs. And this is numbered "1," but it's the second one. It talks about the reaction of the mayor, Radic, at the meeting. Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that as stated in this document that Radic indicated that the situation could get worse with the return of soldiers and refugees to the city?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the situation would get worse, not that it could get worse but that it would get worse for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this something you commonly heard from members of the SDS regarding crimes committed against non-Serbs? In other words, was this blamed on soldiers coming back from the front?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That formulation was often heard. If you have a look at the press, I think you could see that it often appeared in the press too -- in the press in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to the next document, 458. Is it correct that this -- first, can you confirm -- can you tell us who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Club of the Delegates of the SDA and the Bosnian people, who with Mr. Owen compiled this document, and I think it was signed by the president of the Club of Delegates of the SDA. I can recognise it. But I must add one other thing: The document wasn't sent immediately -- it wasn't sent, not immediately, but it wasn't sent soon after Mr. Owen's departure and Mr. Vance, because we wanted a certain period of time to pass to see whether the situation would improve or whether it would deteriorate. So as you see, several months after the meeting, this document was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian. Perhaps you could ask the witness to give us the name of the president of the Club of Delegates of the SDA --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- once he recollects that this document was originally signed by that person.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Djanic. I think that Mr. Djanic signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you read this document before it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you agree with the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this another example of your attempt to inform diplomats in the outside world about crimes that were occurring in your region of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We thought that it would carry its own weight, because Mr. Vance, when he was leaving, he himself suggested that we inform him in the event of the situation deteriorating and in the event of our personal security coming under threat. And we promised Mr. Owen that we would send our response with regard to his request -- we promised that we would send our response in writing. And he requested that we -- that our deputies, our representatives, that they return to the municipal assembly and participate in its work. This was in fact an answer, a reply, to Mr. Owen's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another document, marked P459A in the English and 459B. It's indicated it's from the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade. It's entitled "In the spotlight of the Humanitarian Law Centre, Trebinje, in Banja Luka, dated the 10th of May, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you also speak to members of human rights organisations from various countries, including from Belgrade, from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe that you've been handed the document 459B. Is it correct that you spoke to the authors of this document, and can you tell us whether or not you had seen this document at approximately the time that it was written or distributed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mrs. Natasha Kondic on several occasions, perhaps ten times, who was the president of the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade. We spoke over the phone. In very broad lines, I described to her the situation in Banja Luka and its surroundings. But I didn't go into great detail, which would have been dangerous for me. For example, if I had mentioned the main protagonist, the main criminal protagonists. Mrs. Kondic left the impression of being someone who was really fighting for human rights and was a real humanitarian, a humanist. And in this document, which I subsequently received, not at the time, I was pleasantly surprised, given the precision that the Humanitarian Law Centre -- given the precision that the Humanitarian Law Centre had managed to achieve in this document. And the person who contacted me was really attempting to help the non-Serbian population and to assist in the fight for human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, the documents that we've been talking about discuss your efforts to publicly get the word out to the world about the events that were taking place in the Bosnian Krajina. Isn't it correct that you fought in other ways against the policies of the authorities in Banja Luka during the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to add something, a little detail. I have to say that - please help me with the word - Amnesty International was quite often informed about the situation, especially by the person who was responsible for monitoring violations of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was -- within the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to your efforts, not to inform outsiders about the crimes but to fight against the authorities in power in Banja Luka. Mr. Krzic, did you ever consider or attempt to get weapons to resist the authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But these were individual attempts, so to speak. I was acting in an intuitive way, and it was not with the intention of attacking someone. The intention was that in the case of our lives coming under threat, the intention was to sell our lives for a high price.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you go to both Sarajevo and Zagreb and attempt to get weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to Zagreb with that intention, but I came across the idea in Zagreb to try and get weapons, to try and obtain weapons. Unfortunately, some of the promises came to nothing, in practical terms. There a concrete promise was made in Sarajevo for 40 automatic weapons, for 50 automatic weapons, which we did not receive, but the person who had promised us these weapons was soon after attacked by the State Security Service in Belgrade. He was soon arrested. And the only case in which I managed to obtain weapons involved two old German automatic weapons, which I received in Sarajevo, for my personal protection and in order to protect the Vice-President of the party, to whom I gave that automatic weapon. I took them both to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you -- would it be correct to say that the non-Serbs - and particularly you are probably more familiar with the Muslim population in Banja Luka - probably did have some weapons in their possession in -- within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They obviously did. I am not sure of the exact number. I heard more about it. I heard from the Serbian police when they arrested numerous people. They would often repeat that they knew that we had -- "that you had 2.000 rifles," so this is a rough figure and I really am not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you've indicated that you opposed what the authorities were doing and you saw many, many crimes against the civilian population in that municipality. Why didn't you organise an armed resistance in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, lengthy preparations are necessary for an armed resistance. We hadn't made any such preparations, and no one warned us that we were in danger. When I say that no one warned us, I'm talking about the state authorities. We received no warnings from them. We didn't receive a single document or an order to take certain steps in that direction. There were conversations, there were meetings, relating to that subject but nothing concrete was ever done. When we were faced with -- when our danger -- when our life was really in danger, and I don't mean -- I'm not talking about the possibility of dying accidentally, but I'm talking about the possibility of your family being killed in the course of the day or in the night, which is what happened in -- at various locations, and people who had children were under particular psychological pressure. They could have their children killed before their eyes. This also took place. In such cases, the only thing that a normal person could do, and that includes us too, would be to get his hands on any kind of weapon in order to kill the perpetrator, the criminal, but to kill himself too. This is the only reason for which we tried to get hold of weapons. Obviously, there were groups of youths, of young men, who organised themselves, but these were agreements between young people who played football together, who went to school together, and I have to say that this included both Croats and Bosniaks, but I never saw a single person, a single youth, carrying such a weapon, except for, on several occasions, I saw someone carrying a pistol, a small calibre pistol such as a pistol -- like the pistol that I had. So no intensive preparations took place for us to arm ourselves, but we dreamt about it. We knew that there were individuals, there was a current -- there was a feeling in the population, among the population, a feeling that it shouldn't be used except in the case of mass execution, except in cases where an order of any kind could influence the matter in some way. Killings of certain criminals, of course this occurred in our villages, in our places, but such acts, usually outbursts on our side, revenge would be taken for such acts, and quite disproportionate revenge, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, without giving any names, is it also correct that you had some sources within the military of the VRS, that is the Serbian army in the region, that provided you with information that you, on occasion, passed on to government authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Mr. Krzic, in your estimation, what would have happened if, in 1992, the civilian, non-Serb population in Banja Luka had attempted an uprising against the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was quite clear. There was no dilemma. Intellectuals and non-educated people think in the same way. That would have been a very welcome act, a pretext to take revenge. We were especially bitter because of Mr. Brdjanin and his very dangerous remark, but we were aware that if we did anything against him, a massacre of the entire civilian population would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I just want to clarify some of your language, to make sure which groups you're talking about. I'm reading a little bit of your transcript, and you indicated at one point in the previous question or two questions ago, that "there was a feeling in the population, among the population, a feeling that it shouldn't be used except in the case of mass execution." You're indicating -- can you explain what shouldn't be used and mass execution of what people? I think there may be a little ambiguity there.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will provide you with an example. You know, in Vrbanja, at a meeting in Vrbanja, which was organised at the request of the municipality and which was attended by the mayor, Mr. Radic, and at which an attempt was made in a courteous way to tell the Bosniaks from the Vrbanja settlement -- an attempt was made to state what the problems were. The population, the people who were present there, apologised for putting forth facts on the terror to which they had been exposed, to which they were being exposed in that area of the town. That same evening, participants who had stated these facts, who were -- who felt free to say what had happened, what was happening to them, they were attacked, they were shelled, they were shot at, and they were very happy to escape from the town with their lives. So you can well imagine what would have happened if our people had killed a soldier, not to say a Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In one of your answers, you indicated, when I asked you about an armed uprising, that that would have been a welcome act and a pretext to take revenge. I believe I know what you're talking about but can you please explain who would have welcomed the uprising and used it as a pretext to take revenge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear who would have welcomed that. The greater Serbian forces, as we called them, would have welcomed that. This could include the majority of the members of the SDS at the time, especially members of the Radical Party, as far as the political establishment is concerned. But as far as the military establishment is concerned, we could mention the commanders from that period; we mentioned some of them before. As far as the police is concerned, the heads of the police, who attempted to make such statements. There were attempts to provoke such a revolt, such a rebellion, and I mentioned a book -- I mentioned an event in my book, when the population in the part of the town in which I live was surrounded. That area was surrounded and the population, regardless of their age, this included small children, they were all gathered in Poljakov Park. It's a park called after a well-known family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just want to clarify the language. Is it correct that you're saying that an uprising would have been a pretext used by Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities in power to take revenge against the non-Serb civilian population? Is that your meaning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you know General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have you met him in person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in person on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see him in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you meet with General Talic the first time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was towards the end of May, 1992. I have the exact date here. I don't know if it's necessary for me to find it and to read it out. At the time, people begged for a meeting. They didn't ask for a meeting, but they begged for a meeting with General Talic, the head of the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you met with General Talic -- let's just put that time -- I'm not so much concerned with the exact date but with -- put it in relation to other events. Do you know when that occurred in relation to the attack on Kozarac in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was between -- that was between six and eight days before the attack on Kozarac, that is to say, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The meeting was approximately six to eight days before the attack on Kozarac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was at this meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mufti Halilovic, Professor Osmancevic, Professor Bajric, the economist Safet Filipovic, an old-age pensioner named Dalnezirovic. And I think Professor Bilalbegovic was there, but I'm not exactly sure at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were these all representatives that you've mentioned of the Muslim and Croat communities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, they were the representatives of the Bosniak community, because before that, we had suggested to members of the Croatian community -- we had suggested that we go together. But that was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was discussed -- excuse me. Was General Talic alone, or was he with other individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Talic, Colonel Osman Selak was present and another two or three officers from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you met with General Talic, where did this meeting in the middle of May take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the building of the staff of the Yugoslav army, or it would be better to say in the restaurant which served as -- we simply called it the Dom Armije, "the home of the army" -- on the first floor, in one of the rooms in the corner of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the meeting with General Talic, and what matters did you bring up in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, we wanted this meeting because we hoped that there were certain forces within the army that were capable of protecting the population, protecting them from terror or forms of terror, physical terror, to which the population -- the non-Serbian population was being subjected in Banja Luka and its surroundings. I don't think it is necessary for me to state what this relates to. At the time the first killings, had already taken place. Innocent people had been killed. There was rape and, of course, what we would call culturacide, attacks on culture, on a culture that was very much non-Serbian or that could be considered as European culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there anything about the history of Yugoslavia that made you have some hopes in the army as a force you could talk to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The army was the strongest force. And furthermore, they still insisted -- certain officers in the army still insisted -- still existed who were from the Second World War or were the sons of partisans, fighters in the Second World War. There were still such officers in the Yugoslav army. And we still believed that the army had to be -- had to adhere to the principle that it should not allow such evil being committed against the innocent -- an innocent population and vice versa. We lost any faith in the police, for reasons which I can state later, but this -- these were the last forces that we could count on to protect the population, the non-Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss with General Talic some of the matters that you've just mentioned, that is, crimes against the civilian population and attacks on the culture of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went into detail. I even think that certain things were -- that some things were noted at the place. But you must know that although we were victims, it was necessary to be courageous, to make protests. We were begging for protection. We weren't protesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was General Talic's response when you recounted the crimes that were occurring against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't deny this. He accepted it. I can't even remember that he tried to justify that situation. But he promised that he would form one or two so-called light brigades - and to tell you the truth, maybe I don't know what this means - in order to protect the population, in order to patrol at critical hours -- to patrol in the city at critical hours and, of course, in the villages too. It is true he also warned that he expected even greater trouble in the area of Prijedor. And then we hoped that in the town the situation would become more stable, but we were also concerned about the population in the smaller towns and in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned Prijedor. What did General Talic tell you at this meeting which took place, you said, approximately six or eight days before the attacks on Kozarac about Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to what I've already told you, this is something which he mentioned that -- a meeting in the presence of other people too. When I was leaving, I was in the company of the mufti, and the general showed respect to the mufti. This could be seen from his behaviour. And then when we were on our way out, some people were behind us, and he said once again that in seven days, he expected trouble in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the second meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in about a month or a month and a half time after that. It was then that we held another meeting, also begging to have this meeting organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another document. It has been marked P460. The document indicates it's from the social, cultural, religious, and political associations of the Muslim people in Banja Luka. And it's dated the 22nd of June, 1992 from Banja Luka. It's addressed to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, to General Momir Talic. And it's entitled "Cupertino Proposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, where did the second meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting took place, I think, in the building of the general staff of the army of the time. It was the building next to the Dom Armije.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in front of you, you have the document 460 -- P460B. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is a concept, or rather, a memorandum which we handed over to a group of officers headed by General Talic during our second meeting, which I had to read personally. I'm saying personally because Professor Sirbegovic whose job it was to read it could not -- did not have the energy -- the strength to read it. So the president of the political party was not meant to have read it because we were dealing here with the association of the Bosnian people of Banja Luka. But as he was not able to hold the document in his hand, out of fear I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in this document, did you recount again the crimes and persecution of the non-Serb population in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not list all of them. It was merely a concept, as I mentioned before. But still, there were certain limits which we did not want to overstep in order not to have our physical integrity endangered. We quoted, directly or indirectly, the issue of concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another document we have premarked P461A, it appears on the translation, and 461B on the original. It's entitled at the top, "Item 2, on 22nd June, 1992, talks were held with General Momir Talic," and goes on from there. And on the last page, the second page, appears several signatures. It's ERN number 00923388 and 89 on the English translation. I'd ask these be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in this document 461A-B that's been handed to you, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is this? Can you explain to the Court what it is and how it was written?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled on the same day, on the basis of an agreement amongst the participants of that meeting. I printed it. Everyone received a copy. The five participants. All of him -- all of them were representatives of a part of the Bosniak nation. It was a report of the meeting, our -- one document was the memorandum, and this was a report from that meeting, which we believed was necessary to note down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you had read the proposal for co-operation, did General Talic respond in the way that's indicated in this document? I'm referring to the second page. Did he indicate that he guaranteed the safety of the Banja Luka Muslims and would prevent military forces from engaging in this type of activity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is completely accurate. All of the points listed here are accurate. We were aware of the situation at the time, and there was no question of writing anything down that did not reflect the true state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the second point raised by General Talic, did he -- what did he indicate that the Muslim leadership should do in order to alleviate somewhat the situation in the concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stated then that we should address the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka in connection with visits to the assembly centres and the concentration camps and everything that had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the document that you've -- that you have before you, it actually indicates "Crisis Staff of Banja Luka Municipal Assembly." When you wrote this document, were you -- what was your concept of the number of Crisis Staffs that were in operation in Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, there was only one Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, but as we understood the competence of this staff was that it had had a broader competence, especially in regard to the local Crisis Staffs in other towns and places existing in the area of that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have an idea at that time who was the president of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, one knew who the president of the Crisis Staff was, but since several names were mentioned at the time, I don't know who the president was at the moment, at that particular moment. I know who the members were. According to the Statute of the assembly, it was compulsory for the mayor to be a member of the Crisis Staff. I'm speaking on my own behalf. I was not sure whether it was Mr. Brdjanin who was president of the Crisis Staff or Mr. Radic. So at this particular moment, I cannot really tell. Perhaps they had formal positions, at the time, and perhaps the chief of police was a determining factor, or representative of the General Staff. I cannot really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did General Talic ask you and the other representatives of your community to keep the Muslim population calm within the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Talic, as the other officers did also, on several occasions during our first meeting, and other meetings, he told us that we should remain calm, that the situation would improve. And during one meeting, as far as I know, it may have been the first meeting, one of his associates, Colonel Vukelic, I think his name was, there were young people in the towns that were playing soldiers and that they should be warned not to do so or else they would be arrested. This was in the area of Vrbanja. There was a group called Dobri Jarani, "good friends," that we -- well, we understood that these were young people, that they were having -- that they were trying to play defence. And after the meeting, we went to Vrbanja. We warned those young men that they should not, under any circumstance, play with arms, because this might have been a very costly venture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This warning, in other words --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you can complete your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood the warning in the following way. Young people discuss things, they are in each other's company, and they discuss on how they should fight, but obviously they did not have weapons, because if they had weapons, they would have been immediately arrested. Later on, I found out that these were only physical exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, at each of these meetings, you received -- you've indicated you received promises to protect the civilian population, from General Talic. Did you see any results from these promises? Did the situation and security of the non-Serb civilian population improve following your meetings with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this situation soon deteriorated, increasingly, in the town itself. In the surrounding area, the situation was quite desperate. Information dating to that period reflect that the killings, the looting, the shelling, in the town itself, was -- were daily occurrences. This was a small town, and the information relating to the surroundings reflected that a true genocide was taking place, because mass killings were taking place, and we received reports from even those who managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did General Talic say about the camps in which non-Serbs were being detained in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the talks we had with him, he tried to distinguish, obviously, between the camp in Manjaca, as being a military prisoners' camp, and that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was under the control of the army, whereas, as regards collection centres and prisons and concentration camps, he designated them as places that were under the supervision of the police and obviously of units that did not belong to professional military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the document 461, you wrote that "General Talic said he will send a memorandum to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin of the Public Security Services Centre to release all non-military persons, and he states that conditions there are more difficult than in the military camp." Did that accurately reflect what General Talic told you at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Court what your impression was of General Talic from these meetings, and any other contact you had with him or any other ways you observed him through the media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during our first meeting, actually, I hadn't met General Talic before. The first time I met him was during the first meeting and then during the second meeting. If I can give my personal assessment, during the first meeting, he was -- he still had in him -- he was still carrying in him his affiliation to the Yugoslav nation, that he was still -- he still believed that Yugoslavia would be preserved, that at that that particular point in time, he tried to keep the army outside areas, beyond areas, for which it was not competent for in a situation of war. But I also concluded subsequently, and I wondered -- I asked myself why he was being polite to us, as we were victims where we actually begged for protection. And on the basis of information I had in regard to the situation on the front lines, I understood that his wish was to avoid possible rebellions of the Bosniaks in Banja Luka where military forces would have been involved, which would cause casualties and material destruction. And the Serbian army really required them at the front lines because they were stopped at all the front lines, especially at the corridors, especially in the direction of Jajce, where it suffered casualties. And I received reports about this occasionally. I thought at the time that this was one of the reasons. And today I'm even more convinced of this. Furthermore, I felt that the Serb authorities did not wish to have Banja Luka totally ethnically cleansed, especially not to carry out or to witness massacre killings of the population. This was for political reasons. And I believed that their highest political authorities assessed that such an act would entail international intervention. At a later stage, Mr. Stalic publicly aligned himself with radical political views in regard to the territorial future of that area. He aligned himself totally with the Serb nationalists and did something which we hadn't -- he had never done in the past. He tried to take part in all the religious festivities which had an impact on the Serb population. Through his public acts, he was obviously drawing public attention to the formation of an exclusively Serb army. And as things escalated, he became increasingly explicit in this respect and publicly stated that Serbs and Croats -- that Croats and Bosniaks, actually, had to struggle with the Serbs if the Europeans were to attack the Serbs or they cannot survive amongst the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a convenient time for me to break now, if you wish. I only have -- just to inform the Court and counsel, I have some questions about Mr. Brdjanin, and then I will complete my examination, I think, within about 15 minutes. I've got 15 minutes of direct examination remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After that, Mr. Ackerman, would you be in a position at least to start with the basic introductory questions that you have prepared for the witness on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I had not planned to, but if there's going to be that much time remaining, I can do the best I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either you or Mr. de Roux. I mean, you could sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could utilise the time remaining, that would be appreciated. In the meantime, just for the record purposes, I had the transcript of the hearing of the 21st January brought to me with regard to what I -- what we had agreed. And I am on record here as having said: "So we'll plan to resume on the 13th, unless I have indications that this would be better -- that it would be better to resume on the 14th. But definitely it will be either the 13th or the 14th. For the moment, it's the 13th." So that seems to be the position as we had agreed upon it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the younger mind at work. You remember correctly, and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's machinery at work. Yes, Mr. de Roux.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to avoid ambiguities, I must tell the Court that I will not be present on the 13th because I will be in hospital then, and I think I shall return on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. de Roux. This is how it should be. However, please do make sure that your co-counsel is present. It's very important. Otherwise -- my message yesterday -- if it wasn't clear enough, I will repeat it today. Don't ever put this Trial Chamber in a position where accused -- your client will stand up and says, "I don't want the hearing to continue today because I am not assisted by the counsel and co-counsel assigned me." There I will fall on you, and you'll never know what hit you. So it's -- but otherwise, as long as we do things as they should, there will be no problems. So we will resume in 25 minutes' time. I understand that you will conclude your examination-in-chief and that either Mr. Ackerman or Mr. de Roux will commence the cross-examination. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Bring in the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Krzic, counsel, Mr. Koumjian, for the Prosecution will resume his cross-examination -- his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just mention, Mr. Cayley asked me to ask the Trial Chamber for about ten minutes at the end of today's session to address some issues with the Court regarding scheduling and other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you ever meet Radoslav Brdjanin or see him in person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe those occasions where you saw Mr. Brdjanin in person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It usually took place in the building of the municipal assembly or in the Home of Culture where these sessions, the sessions of the municipal assembly, were held. Direct meeting with him perhaps took place on several occasions. I remember that the first time was when it was the Orthodox New Year or Christmas. This also took place in the Dom Kultura, the Home of Culture, where the SDS party had organised a reception. Another close encounter was in the Hotel Bosna, with the co-president of the Security Council, Mr. Vance Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You're speaking about the Vance-Owen delegation which came to Banja Luka to discuss a possible solution to the crisis in Bosnia; is that correct? That would be Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe where it was that you saw Mr. Brdjanin in relation to the Vance-Owen delegation trip to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Brdjanin on the first floor, in the lounge of the hotel, which is completely open. It is not partitioned. Not only Mr. Brdjanin but Karadzic, Kupresanin, all the heads, all the highest ranking heads of the authorities at that time. I can't remember whether Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic were there at the time. I saw Mr. Brdjanin when I entered, speaking with the co-president, and then during a pause when Mr. Vance sent me to call my collaborators, my colleagues from the municipal assembly, which is about 100 metres from there, and I then approached the secretary of the municipality, Mr. Tihic, and asked him that he personally or someone else call some of the people from the -- of the leading -- of the leaders in the municipality, that Mr. Brdjanin suddenly got up, came between me and Mr. Tihic, and he was suggesting that he didn't support my request. Then Mr. Vance's personal secretary appeared. I approached him. I spoke to him and said that they wouldn't listen to me and that they wouldn't call the other members of the delegates. That was the meeting I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, you were going to attempt to arrange a meeting between members of the Muslim community, representatives and leaders, with Mr. Vance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not completely correct. I wasn't trying to organise it. But the meeting with representatives of the SDA party, so not of the entire Bosniak community but only the members of the SDA party, and myself, this meeting was requested by Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, but when I was received by them, I asked them to call some other members of the executive committee of the SDA because I thought that this was necessary for such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Brdjanin in court today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you just point out where he's sitting now.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I indicate that with my finger or how?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he's sitting next to or where he's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin is sitting next to General Talic. He is on his right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin on television or in other forms of media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him on television many times. And on several occasions, I heard him speaking on Banja Luka radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the statements that you heard Mr. Brdjanin make on television or radio?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Brdjanin was -- could be heard in the media after he had been elected as the president of the SDA party in Celinac, or as far as I can remember, the elections for the -- to the main council of the SDA -- SDS. He appeared very often. But what is important is that there was always a certain political edge to his appearances. And for our Bosniaks what is very important is that he made continual threats against the non-Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges of this Trial Chamber and try to tell us your best recollection of the words that Mr. Brdjanin used and what you -- and why you feel that these constituted threats.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I failed to say that Mr. Brdjanin in our personal meetings -- when we would meet personally, he would never even greet me. But that's not important now. But if we're talking about the vocabulary that he used, the words that he used in his interviews, whether he was being interviewed on his own or whether he was with others, his range of vocabulary was such that this was Serbian territory and that everything that the Serbian army seized would remain in the hands of the Serbs, it would be their property, and that there was no life for non-Serbians, apart from a negligible number. And in Banja Luka, this was between a thousand and 2.000 people, not even 1 per cent. In certain stages -- at certain stages, he made some very dangerous remarks, dangerous statements, to the effect that the non-Serbian population were worms, lice, insects that had to be trodden on. He condemned Serbs who did anything to facilitate the survival or even the departure from Banja Luka of the non-Serbian population. A well-known remark of his, which is when he attacked the Serbians who had enabled Bosniaks to obtain false documents in order to leave Banja Luka -- at one point in time, it was impossible for non-Serbs to leave Banja Luka -- he said that this was a crime being committed by such Serbs. But in the end he justified it because he said there will be less non-Serbs in this area in the end. He said this publicly. Furthermore, he would sometimes say that the Bosniaks and Croats were subversive elements. Such a statement -- it could be said that we were -- that we could be -- he didn't make a distinction between people, between their age -- on the base of their age, their sex, and on the base of whether certain people had been prominent in certain situations. You can imagine what his positions were. Such statements, in our opinion, represented the threat of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These statements that you're talking about, are these statements that you personally heard Mr. Brdjanin make on the television or radio?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some of the statements personally, and some of them I read in the newspapers. What I heard from other people, I don't think it's necessary to mention that because the register is more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document that has been marked -- pre-marked P462A for the English translation and B for the original in B/C/S. It is indicated it's from the Party of Democratic Action, Banja Luka, dated 28 August 1992. It appears to be sent to the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations in New York, addressed to Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey personally. And it indicates a short report of events, beginning at the first paragraph: "Yesterday, 27th August 1992 an interview was held on Banja Luka TV."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you've been handed a copy of this document, 462. Can you first tell us who wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The first paragraph of this document discusses a television show on Banja Luka TV. Do you recall this television show?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do, but I couldn't -- I'm not in a position to reproduce it in its entirety at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you wrote this document, was the -- were the events that you had seen on the television show fresh in your memory? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that very same evening, I made some notes, and this document was sent to the authorities on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you read through this document and tell me if you find it to be, to the best of your recollection today, an accurate record of what you saw on the television on the 27th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an accurate record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, given all of the comments by Mr. Brdjanin that you have told us about today, in your opinion, did these comments have an effect upon the feelings of the non-Serb population regarding their security in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There is no doubt about that. Not only did it create a feeling of insecurity, but we thought that this was also an open invitation to potential criminals, an open invitation to them to freely do what they had already been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "what they had already been doing," can you, for the record, specify what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of all the acts of terrorism which had been perpetrated, from simple beatings, arrests, killings, rape, looting, expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did these remarks, public remarks, by Mr. Brdjanin, facilitate the removal of the non-Serbian population from the region?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of implications it had, in terms of the practical implementation of the measures by the Serbian authorities, but I do know that there were additional -- there was an additional burden on the non-Serbian population in the sense that some things were being encouraged and having them removed, deported, was being encouraged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. However, I do have one document, 449; we previously provided only the translation, and I do have the original B/C/S version which has been marked P449B. Just for the record again, this is a -- indicates -- I'm trying to translate quickly, in my limited capacity, from the original, but it's from the SDA party, Banja Luka, dated September 30th, 1992, to the Bosnian mission at the United Nations, and the ERN number 02098593. May this document, in the original B/C/S, be marked P449B and will the Trial Chamber accept that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I understand you have finished your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was -- Mr. Ackerman and Mr. de Roux --

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am -- if the Chamber agrees, I am ready to start with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was going to suggest, that since you are not going to be here on the 13th, that you would commence the cross-examination, the first cross-examination, and then Mr. Ackerman will follow afterwards. Hopefully, between today and tomorrow, I would expect you to finish your cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Might I suggest, before we begin, that Mr. Cayley take up what he says is a ten-minute thing? Because those always turn out to be 15 or 20 minute things. If we can go past 1.45, that's not a problem. If we can't, he probably should be permitted to have his say and make sure we have ample time to deal with it. That's up to Your Honours. That's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can actually start with the -- that would entail the witness having to go out and having to come in again, so I would prefer Mr. de Roux to start with the cross-examination now. Restrict, please, your cross-examination to the preliminaries, and then obviously you will go into more detail tomorrow when the witness will be here with us again, and then you will have the -- roughly you have a quarter of an hour, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you were the President of the SDA in Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992. Could you tell us in brief what the programme was, or the objective, at least, of the SDA during this period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the President, as you say. The objectives of the SDA were contained in the -- its programme. Would you like me to mention some of them now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will mention the ones that I can remember the best. One of the objectives was to help the development of democracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say in the former Yugoslavia, and, as part of this objective, to democratically secure, and to assist in the normal development of, a democratic society, and the accent was especially on the Bosniak population, which up until then did not have the possibility, the full possibilities, of developing in that direction. That was one of our objectives. Another one was that homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was also the homeland of other peoples, and that all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be equal and have equal rights. Naturally, I am speaking in very general terms, and I can't be very precise, but these were certain positions which --

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: But your party had certain religious aspects, should we say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But one of its positions was that we should -- that we would respect the religious convictions of people. This was emphasised because we had just come out of a communist system where the reverse was the case, there was pressure, and there was not much freedom for religious expression. But we didn't have any religious symbols. Even our name, as you can see, doesn't suggest anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: What was the influence of Mr. Izetbegovic's thoughts on the party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Izetbegovic, acting within our political group, in the course of the foundation of the party, while the party was being founded, he was a fairly -- he wasn't a very well-known figure. He was perhaps known to the population as someone who had been expelled from the system at the time, as a victim of the system at that time, because of his religious convictions. But only at a later date, having read his works, only then was it possible to say that Mr. Izetbegovic grew in stature, his image grew in stature. I cannot personally say that Mr. Izetbegovic exerted an influence in any sense, exerted a particular influence on the formation of the party in Banja Luka, and especially not on the way in which it operated. If there was any kind of influence, it might have been an influence that was exerted over certain members of the SDA, like Mr. Filipovic, Professor Muhamed Filipovic, or an influence over Zulfikarpasic, Mr. Zulfikarpasic. It is possible that these members, at the time that division was being created within the SDA, at a time when the MBO organisation was formed, it is possible that one of those members joined that organisation. Finally, the SDA party in Banja Luka, the first president, who was elected by acclamation, Hamza Mujagic, joined the MBO party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Did you -- have you personally read his book, "The Declaration on Islam"? I'm talking about Mr. Izetbegovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, I have not read it. I didn't read it until very late, maybe that was in 1994, I can't remember the exact year, but I think I read it -- I think in the spring of 1992, when I was visiting Sarajevo, I visited, to the extent that this was possible in a couple of days, I read his work, "Islam Between the East and the West," that is, "Islam, a Bridge Between the East and the West."

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Thank you. For a long time, you were a militant in the Communist League. You played a role within that party. So one might think that you were in favour of the Federation of Yugoslavia, that you had been educated with this idea of a federal Yugoslavia in mind. What made you adhere to, let's say, this independence movement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said corresponds to what I said earlier on about my previous political involvement, except for the fact that I entered the Communist League of Yugoslavia at quite a -- at a fairly late date, and I remained in that league for a short period of time, in fact. I also said that the reason -- the main reason for leaving the Communist Party was the fact that -- the concept of a big nationalist idea was more and more prevalent in the Communist Party. As an example, I will mention, when I entered the Communist Party, there was a principle - it was almost an axiom - according to which all positions and responsibility in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in companies, in institutions, in society, in sports clubs too, and in cultural institutions, in such institutions it was important to respect the so-called national key, which in general terms corresponded to the composition of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We respected this, and it was a symbol for us which told us that we were all equal citizens in Yugoslavia. I personally supported Yugoslavia as a state from this position: as a state which consisted of several republics. However, with the decline of communism, or rather, when these ideas of a greater Serbia were being put forward and at a stage when the central communist -- when the central authorities -- when the federal representatives of the Communist Parties, which includes their representatives in the state organs, when this negative aspect became apparent here too, when it became apparent that at the level of the Presidency, there was a movement for a greater Serbia, when it was obvious that the Presidency of Yugoslavia did not respect the equality of all peoples and all republics, when it became obvious that provocations at mass meetings at which greater Serbian statements would be made, when this became obvious and we saw that they were turning Yugoslavia into a dungeon for the people -- although I know that Bosniaks in the former Yugoslavia were not quite equal -- it was only then, it was only at that stage that my positions changed and I became -- I started to support the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I wasn't an elected representative, so I couldn't participate in this, in a body of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Do you believe the attempt to change Yugoslavia into a dungeon was after the death of Marsal Tito?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned earlier on that this idea had evolved earlier on, ten years prior to Tito's death. This was quite evident that President Tito had failing health and that he was obviously losing his leadership role on strategic matters and decisions within Yugoslavia. He had not prepared the country for democratic changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: Well, let us not speak of history any more, because we have cleared up certain issues in that respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would -- if it's convenient for you, Mr. de Roux, I would stop here, so that we dedicate the next ten minutes to organisational matters. And you will be able to resume your cross-examination tomorrow. In the meantime, the witness will remain in the same position he is now. Kindly be present here tomorrow morning at 9.00 so that the cross-examination by Defence teams will take place. I think the witness can leave the room

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krzic. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to very briefly raise three matters with the Chamber. The first is in respect of witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The timing that has being given by my learned colleagues for the Defence, Mr. Ackerman believes he will take the best part of a session. I'm not sure whether Mr. de Roux gave a similar indication. They've already made it clear to you, and I accept that, that cross-examination is often difficult to plan how long it's going to take, but that may leave us with one session or part of a session, depending on how long the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very likely, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will, for the reasons you stated yesterday, have to call Mr. Inayat in respect of the documents for the Banja Luka collection. What I'm asking you is whether or not you wish us to bring another witness, another, in fact, Bosnian witness who will effectively start his evidence on Thursday and then have to return to Bosnia to be brought back again on Sunday, or stay here for those three days, to commence his testimony again on the following Monday. We can do that, but I simply bring it to your attention to explain to you the difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are doing the right thing to bring this up to the Chamber's attention. I personally -- but I obviously will consult the other two Judges. I personally do not see any sense in bringing the witness on Thursday not even knowing whether that witness will be giving evidence on that day and then having him return to wherever he is coming from and then brought again to The Hague on Monday. I don't think it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think my colleagues are in agreement with what I have just stated. What I would suppose is that -- have Mr. Inayat prepared, assuming that there will be time for his evidence, because anything could happen. We could not finish the cross-examination. As I take it, Mr. de Roux requires a full session and Mr. Ackerman requires a full session plus a part of another, so more or less we're talking of a full day -- a full session tomorrow, then a full session on Wednesday of next week, part of Thursday. And that is if everything goes smoothly, as planned. If the witness takes too long to answer questions or if the witness is made to ask -- to answer questions which are in themselves provocative of further cross-examination, I would anticipate that we could easily go until the end of Thursday. So bringing a witness, I think, is -- doesn't make sense. It's not a practical -- let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll proceed on that basis. The next matter I'd like to raise with the Court is that of documents, again. The Banja Luka collection consists of over 400 documents, as you've already seen from the copies that Your Honours have in your possession. As I indicated to the Court earlier this week, my learned friends from the Defence have already given indication of those which they object to. The vast majority of the documents that are objected to -- and I've counted them. It's 71. There are other categories, but the biggest category consists of 71 documents, which are objected to in terms of admission of those documents. The admission into evidence at all of those documents is objected to upon the basis of lack of signatures or stamps or because they do not come from a reliable source, which then, of course, triggers the witness having to come in and explain where we got those documents from. I still sense, Your Honours, a sort of lack of clarity of thought between the Defence, probably on my part as well, about this whole issue of the distinction between admissibility and probative value. And I know you did state that you would issue at some stage a written decision on this matter, on documentary evidence. And I would simply respectfully say that I think that would be extraordinarily helpful, if we had a written decision to look to when this issue arises, which it will constantly arise in the course of the trial, because some of the other categories that are identified here, objections as to authenticity -- and authenticity from my understanding of the previous decision goes to weight and probative value. It doesn't go to admission of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct, Mr. Cayley. Actually, what I have done is that I have handed to one of my legal officers the points that I dealt with when I gave the -- when we gave the oral decision earlier on last week, with the understanding that they had to -- the legal team then had to elaborate a written decision for us to go through and make sure that it is in conformity with the oral decision that was handed down last week. These points, as you rightly point out, are included in -- and will definitely feature in the written -- in the written decision. Definitely this Trial Chamber is attaching to this matter great importance, and that is why, rather than leaving it as an oral decision, we are incorporating it in a written one, because it will be there and it will supposedly guide you. But, however, if I need to repeat the point again - and I would be prepared to repeat it ad nauseam - please do not confuse the initial stage of admission of documents for the purposes of evidence with the stage of going into the probative value or the relevance. It is obvious that at the initial stage, when either you, as Prosecutor, or Mr. Ackerman or Maitre de Roux, as counsel for either one or the other of the accused in this trial, comes forward with a document to which there is an objection, a document which is disputed, at that very early stage, what the Trial Chamber will go into is not -- is nothing else but whether there are, on a prima facie basis, what has previously been referred to as indicia of reliability. If we are definitely looking at a fake document, a document which, on the face of it, very obviously cannot be a reliable document, has absolutely no indicia of reliability, then obviously, that will be taken into account and that, even at that very early stage, it will not be admitted in evidence. However, as I tried to explain yesterday, if I remember well - or not yesterday, on Friday - the position as you should consider it as regulating our future -- our work presently and in future is the following: If there is a document to which an objection has been communicated to you, then you should provide, as early as possible, even before the Trial Chamber is made aware of the existence of this document, you should provide a chart or a list, which I understand will be prepared with the help of Mr. Inayat, indicating the source of this document. Now, it is obvious that if there is no source, the question of admissibility, even at that very early stage, can present you with some difficulties. If there is a source, then the Defence, or it could be you for that matter, will have a clear indication of what the source is, and the moment it is put in front of the three Judges forming -- constituting this Trial Chamber, we would be in a position to know whether, as far as we are concerned, we would require evidence from anyone to give us details, because it could well be that on the basis of what we have already decided, both Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux will not raise any complaints any further, will just have it on record that they still object to the admission of those documents, those documents would still be admitted because, on the face of the record, there is a source indicated, and in the absence of an apparent reason, at least, why we should doubt the credibility and reliability of that source, we would admit that document, and the story commences from there or continues from there. I thought we had made ourselves clear enough. Obviously, I may not have been as clear as I thought I had been. However, this is how we should move. And I also made it clear that at this very early stage, I was reserving the right, to whichever party is objecting or disputing the reliability or the authenticity of those documents, to cross-examine or ask to cross-examine Mr. Inayat, or whoever it will be, limitedly, to the reliability of that source, certainly not as to the content, relevance or probative value of those documents. Those obviously were -- those elements will come into play at a later stage. But at the very early stage of admission -- deciding to admit these documents, this is what you have to worry about: Provide the corresponding, the other, party, with at least an indication of the source, making it possible for the other party and for the Trial Chamber to reach some preliminary -- make some preliminary ideas -- have some preliminary ideas as to how reliable that source could be. If you are in doubt, or if we are in doubt, then there are going to be problems. If the source is like the source or similar to the sources that you had in the case of the documents that were in the two binders that were made use of by Dr. Donia in his evidence, then obviously there are not going to be problems with regard to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, I understand you perfectly and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have a written decision obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand you perfectly, but if I could just clarify from the Defence perspective, because they do have a list identifying the sources of these documents from the Banja Luka collection, if their objection is based principally on lack of signature or stamps or because the source is unreliable, then we will bring in Mr. Inayat to go through those 70 documents that are disputed, explain to the court where they come from and then he can be cross-examined on that evidence as to the reliability of the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Probably at that point in time, the Trial Chamber will take Mr. Inayat in our hands and ask him to confirm what is indicated as being the sources for each and every one of those 72 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents, sorry. You would not be expected to put any questions yourselves to Mr. Inayat. It's up to the Defence if they contest the source's reliability, on a prima facie basis, to cross-examine Mr. Inayat on those 72 documents or on some of them or on none of them. So that is the position. I think I had made it clear yesterday. I apologise to you if I had not. Yes, Mr. Ackerman? You're going to tell me that I had made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have made yourself abundantly clear, at least four times now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I have never failed to understand what it is your position is, and the entire Chamber's position is, with regard to these documents. My learned colleagues don't like your ruling, and so they keep bringing it up, hoping you will change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seriously object to Mr. Ackerman suggesting that I dislike or like something that this Court has decided. I have here his fax in front of me where he is stating that he objects to these documents because they don't come from a reliable source. That is what I'm responding to. It's not whether I like or dislike a decision of the Chamber. I'm simply doing my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you can rest assured that this Chamber would be very little troubled if it came to know that you are -- you don't like its ruling. It won't make any difference. Anyway, we will proceed according to that ruling. However, point taken, you were right in objecting to the remark made by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be short because we are keeping the interpreters here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will not say another word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maitre de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further points?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will adjourn until tomorrow. Tomorrow's sitting is here in this same courtroom, at 9.00 sharp. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.52 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of February, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
